title: Screwworm Wildlife Monitoring: The Blind Spot on Feral Hog Lines
content:
Screwworm wildlife monitoring covers the feral hog line that cattle checks cannot see. Cattle monitoring and wildlife monitoring are different jobs. During a New World screwworm alert, landowners may inspect herds and check fresh wounds. They may follow a clear reporting path while feral hog lines and wildlife crossings continue moving without anyone watching.

This is a screwworm wildlife monitoring problem, not a clinical guide. USDA APHIS explains that screwworm targets live animals with fresh wounds, not feces. Trap-site observation can show where feral hogs are active. It cannot diagnose a case. If you suspect screwworm in cattle, wildlife, or feral hogs, contact USDA APHIS. Contact your state agricultural extension office.

Why Cattle and Wildlife Coverage Diverge

Cattle are visible and handled. A team can walk a pasture. The team can examine an animal, document a wound, and involve a veterinarian. Feral hogs and other wildlife are not on that schedule. They move when the team is away. They move through brush. They fight. They cross fences. They return to bait after dark. A cattle check does not tell you what used the back fence last night.

That creates two parallel systems. Managed livestock has scheduled checks and known contacts. Unmanaged wildlife has no inspection routine. Build observation around the places where animals concentrate. Screwworm wildlife monitoring does not mean inspecting every deer. It means not treating the hog line as covered simply because the herd was checked that morning.

The Hog Line Is a Practical Observation Point

Trap lines already sit in wildlife corridors. Fresh rooting, trails, wallows, bait, and water bring sounders back to the same ground. A camera at that point can show which animals use the site. It gives a current view. It can show when activity changes. It can show whether a catch changed pressure. It can also show whether a catch reduced pressure or shifted it to another crossing.

Weekly drives provide delayed information. Live trap-site monitoring provides a current view without asking the team to visit every site at night. It also keeps the purpose clear: the system supports trap monitoring, closure timing, and sounder capture. It is not a veterinary substitute.

What Observation Can and Cannot Show

  • Confirm when feral hogs are active at a monitored trap site
  • Help separate hog activity from other wildlife around bait
  • Support whole-sounder removal by showing when the group is committed
  • Give your team movement context for a discussion with an agency or extension contact

A camera cannot show larvae, confirm an infestation, or tell you to treat an animal. Keep suspected cases on the agency reporting path. A trap log can record the date, location, species if known, sounder estimate, and catch outcome. It remains an operations record.

Align Cattle Protocols With Trap-Line Coverage

Run the two tracks together. Do not duplicate them. Keep normal livestock checks and wound reporting in place. Add a daily remote review for active trap sites. Increase that review during heightened alert periods. Keep a weekly sounder log and name a backup operator who can send the closure command when the primary reviewer is unavailable.

A wild hog trap camera system should show the entry, the inside of the trap, and the approach area. The HogEye steel camera is designed for that trap-site job. It supports the trap view. Installation references are available in camera resources.

Trapping Outcomes Matter to Both Tracks

Whole-sounder removal lowers the number of wide-ranging hogs crossing the property. Those animals are otherwise unwatched. Remote monitoring helps the team wait until the full sounder is inside and settled before sending a closure command. Partial captures educate survivors and may move activity into a corridor with no camera.

After a catch, review the feed and the log. Did the entire sounder enter? Did another group replace it? Did activity move toward a fence gap or water edge? Those answers make the wildlife side of the property less dependent on guesswork.

When to Escalate

Contact USDA APHIS and your state extension office if you suspect screwworm. Record what you saw, where you saw it, and when. Do not diagnose or treat from camera footage. HogEye Mini is $1,299. Frequently Asked Questions

What is screwworm wildlife monitoring on a hog line?

It is continuous observation at trap sites and crossings where feral hogs and other wildlife concentrate, while agency partners handle diagnosis and reporting.

Can a trap camera identify screwworm?

No. It shows movement and supports trapping decisions. Confirmation belongs to USDA APHIS and your state extension office.

Why start with feral hog lines?

Hogs are wide-ranging, frequently wounded, and largely unmonitored. Trap sites are where they already concentrate, so observation can close a high-value gap.
